claim: Studies on starlings (Pompilio and Kacelnik, 2010) and humans (Bavard et al., 2018; Bavard et al., 2021; Klein et al., 2017) demonstrated that both absolute memories and remembered ranking are combined in particular ways to give rise to these animals' preferences.
source: Studies on starlings (Pompilio and Kacelnik, 2010) and humans (Bavard et al., 2018; Bavard et al., 2021; Klein et al., 2017) demonstrated that both absolute memories and remembered ranking are combined in particular ways to give rise to these animals' preferences.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on starlings and humans.

claim: Bumblebees' learned preferences are based only on memories of ordinal comparisons.
source: We show that bumblebees' learned preferences are based only on memories of ordinal comparisons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript (experiments 1-6).

claim: After learning to discriminate pairs of different flowers by sucrose concentration, bumblebees preferred flowers (in novel pairings) with higher ranking over equal absolute reward.
source: A series of experiments showed that after learning to discriminate pairs of different flowers by sucrose concentration, bumblebees preferred flowers (in novel pairings) with (1) higher ranking over equal absolute reward
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from experiment 1 as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: After learning to discriminate pairs of different flowers by sucrose concentration, bumblebees preferred flowers (in novel pairings) with higher ranking over higher absolute reward.
source: A series of experiments showed that after learning to discriminate pairs of different flowers by sucrose concentration, bumblebees preferred flowers (in novel pairings) with (1) higher ranking over equal absolute reward, (2) higher ranking over higher absolute reward
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from experiment 2 as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After learning to discriminate pairs of different flowers by sucrose concentration, bumblebees preferred flowers with identical qualitative ranking but different quantitative ranking equally.
source: A series of experiments showed that after learning to discriminate pairs of different flowers by sucrose concentration, bumblebees preferred flowers (in novel pairings) with (1) higher ranking over equal absolute reward, (2) higher ranking over higher absolute reward, and (3) identical qualitative ranking but different quantitative ranking equally.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from experiment 3 as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Bumblebees used absolute information in order to rank different flowers.
source: Bumblebees used absolute information in order to rank different flowers.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that bees could discriminate and rank flowers during training, which requires processing absolute information.

claim: When ranking information was absent (i.e. bees learned one flower at a time), memories for absolute information were lost or could no longer be retrieved after at most 1 hr.
source: However, additional experiments revealed that, even when ranking information was absent (i.e. bees learned one flower at a time), memories for absolute information were lost or could no longer be retrieved after at most 1 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from experiment 4 as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Animals' choices can be influenced by the presence of additional options.
source: Under such conditions, a wealth of research shows that animals' choices can be influenced by the presence of additional options (Hunter and Daw, 2021; Spektor et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Contextual effects on direct assessments have been found across the animal kingdom, including humans and other primates, bats, birds, frogs, fish, bees, and worms.
source: Evidence of contextual effects like this on direct assessments has been found across the animal kingdom, e.g. humans and other primates (Berkowitsch et al., 2014; Parrish et al., 2015; Trueblood et al., 2013), bats (Hemingway et al., 2021), birds (Bateson, 2002; Morgan et al., 2012), frogs (Lea and Ryan, 2015), fish (Reding and Cummings, 2017), bees (Shafir et al., 2002), and worms (Iwanir et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research across different species.

claim: Little is known about the type and degree of information (absolute and/or relative) that is encoded in the remembered subjective values of options.
source: However, little is known about the type and degree of information (absolute and/or relative) that is encoded in the remembered subjective values of options.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in scientific knowledge as stated by the authors.

claim: No species other than starlings and humans have been investigated for the roles played by absolute memories and remembered ranking in learned preferences.
source: So far, however, no other species have been investigated for the roles played by absolute memories and remembered ranking in learned preferences.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature as stated by the authors.

claim: Bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) are a key model for examining the economy of decision-making outside of humans.
source: Here, we examine this in bumblebees (Bombus terrestris), an invertebrate and a key model for examining the economy of decision-making outside of humans (Real, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The sucrose concentrations A:B=45%:30% had the same perceived difference as C:D=30%:20% according to Weber's Law.
source: The sucrose concentrations of the different pairs of flowers were chosen according to Weber's Law (Akre and Johnsen, 2014) to represent the same perceived difference, i.e. A:B=45%:30% had the same contrast of incentives as C:D=30%:20% (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on Weber's Law as cited and the experimental design.

claim: In experiment 1, bees significantly preferred C over B in an unrewarding test (generalised linear model [GLM]: 95% CI = [0.08, 0.38], N=40, and p=4.00e-3).
source: In an unrewarding test with B and C flowers, bees significantly preferred C over B (generalised linear model [GLM]: 95% CI = [0.08, 0.38], N=40, and p=4.00e-3; Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The preference for C over B in experiment 1 suggests that bees store memories for the relative ranking of flowers.
source: Although these results suggest that bees store memories for the relative ranking of flowers, they still may encode absolute information (Table 1), and therefore, we carried out additional experiments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 1.

claim: In experiment 2, bees preferred C over B (GLM: 95% CI = [0.07, 0.28], N=40, and p=3.30e-3).
source: Similar to experiment 1, the result of the unrewarding test showed that bees preferred C (GLM: 95% CI = [0.07, 0.28], N=40, and p=3.30e-3; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was no significant difference in preference for C across experiments 1 and 2 (GLM: 95% CI = [–0.24, 0.13], N=80, and p=0.55).
source: There was no significant difference in preference for C across experiments 1 and 2 (GLM: 95% CI = [–0.24, 0.13], N=80, and p=0.55; Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of data from experiments 1 and 2.

claim: There is no evidence that bumblebees' choices in novel contexts are based on remembered absolute metrics.
source: There is thus no evidence that bumblebees' choices in novel contexts are based on remembered absolute metrics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of difference between experiments 1 and 2.

claim: In experiment 3, bees chose A and C equally (GLM: 95% CI = [–0.16, 0.12], N=40, and p=0.79).
source: In the unrewarding test, bees chose A and C equally (GLM: 95% CI = [–0.16, 0.12], N=40, and p=0.79; Figure 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The equal preference for A and C in experiment 3 suggests bumblebees store and recall only memories for the qualitative difference between options.
source: In the unrewarding test, bees chose A and C equally (GLM: 95% CI = [–0.16, 0.12], N=40, and p=0.79; Figure 1F), suggesting bumblebees store and recall only memories for the qualitative difference between options.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 3.

claim: Bumblebees' lack of preference for the equally ranked A and C flowers, despite their difference in sugar concentration, demonstrates absolute memories were not remembered.
source: Furthermore, bumblebees' lack of preference for the equally ranked A and C flowers, despite their difference in sugar concentration, demonstrates absolute memories were not remembered (Table 1)
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 3.

claim: The results of experiments 1, 2, and 3 together suggest that bumblebees only encode and recall remembered ranking for use in novel contexts.
source: Furthermore, bumblebees' lack of preference for the equally ranked A and C flowers, despite their difference in sugar concentration, demonstrates absolute memories were not remembered (Table 1) and, in combination with experiments 1 and 2, suggests that bumblebees only encode and recall remembered ranking for use in novel contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of experiments 1, 2, and 3.

claim: In experiment 4, bees had no significant preferences for either option (GLM: 95% CI = [–0.15, 0.22], N=20, and p=0.69).
source: However, bees had no significant preferences for either option (GLM: 95% CI = [–0.15, 0.22], N=20, and p=0.69; Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Bees' lack of absolute memory in the tests of experiments 1–3 was unlikely to be a result of absolute memories being less salient and overshadowed by ranking memories.
source: However, bees had no significant preferences for either option (GLM: 95% CI = [–0.15, 0.22], N=20, and p=0.69; Figure 2B), suggesting that bees' lack of absolute memory in the tests of experiments 1–3 was unlikely to be a result of absolute memories being less salient and overshadowed by ranking memories.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 4.

claim: In experiment 5, bees preferred the option that had offered the higher sugar concentration in training (GLM: 95% CI = [0.23, 0.87], N=10, and p=8.29e-3).
source: During the unrewarded test, bees preferred the option that had offered the higher sugar concentration in training (GLM: 95% CI = [0.23, 0.87], N=10, and p=8.29e-3; Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Absolute information about a flower learned in visual isolation can be retained by bumblebees for at least a couple of minutes.
source: During the unrewarded test, bees preferred the option that had offered the higher sugar concentration in training (GLM: 95% CI = [0.23, 0.87], N=10, and p=8.29e-3; Figure 2D), suggesting that absolute information about a flower learned in visual isolation can be retained for at least a couple of minutes but, as experiment 4 highlights, is eventually lost or not able to be recalled later.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 5.

claim: Experiments 4 and 5 collectively indicate that bumblebees can use absolute information to compare options only in their short-term memories (range of minutes) but not in their mid-term memories (range of hours).
source: Experiment 4 and 5 thus collectively indicate that bumblebees can use absolute information to compare options only in their short-term memories (range of minutes) but not in their mid-term memories (range of hours; Menzel, 2001).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of experiments 4 and 5, with reference to established knowledge about bee memory.

claim: In the wild, bumblebees often forage in situations whereby when drinking from one flower type they cannot see other flower types in their field of view.
source: In the wild, bumblebees often forage in situations whereby when drinking from one flower type they cannot see other flower types in their field of view, i.e. on the other side of a bush or many meters away.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about bumblebee foraging behavior.

claim: The distance between any two flowers within a bumblebee's foraging range can be traversed within minutes.
source: Yet, the distance between any two flowers within a bumblebee's foraging range can be traversed within minutes (Osborne et al., 1999), i.e. within the range of bumblebees' short-term memories (Menzel, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on bumblebee foraging and memory.

claim: In experiment 6, bees preferred option A in the unrewarding test with all four options available (GLM: 95% CI = [0.94, 1.68], N=20, and p=1.21e-6).
source: In the unrewarding test with all four options available, bees preferred option A (GLM: 95% CI = [0.94, 1.68], N=20, and p=1.21e-6; Figure 2F)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The short retention/utilisation of absolute memories that bumblebees showed in lab-created situations are likely not to be disadvantageous to bumblebees in the wild, given their natural behaviour and ecological niche.
source: In the unrewarding test with all four options available, bees preferred option A (GLM: 95% CI = [0.94, 1.68], N=20, and p=1.21e-6; Figure 2F), indicating that the short retention/utilisation of absolute memories that bumblebees showed in our lab-created situations are likely not to be disadvantageous to bumblebees in the wild, given their natural behaviour and ecological niche.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 6 in relation to natural foraging behavior.

claim: Bumblebees are only able to make use of ordinal ranking memories to guide foraging choices outside their original learning contexts.
source: Our results suggest that bumblebees are only able to make use of ordinal ranking memories to guide foraging choices outside their original learning contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental results presented.

claim: Absolute information is essential for any animal to compare any two options initially.
source: Although absolute information is essential for any animal to compare any two options initially, our findings show that only ordinal ranking can be recalled by bumblebees later in new contexts.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about how animals process comparative information.

claim: Only ordinal ranking can be recalled by bumblebees later in new contexts.
source: Although absolute information is essential for any animal to compare any two options initially, our findings show that only ordinal ranking can be recalled by bumblebees later in new contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental results presented.

claim: Temporal adjacency is necessary for absolute information of different options to be compared by bees.
source: Our results suggest that temporal adjacency is necessary for absolute information of different options to be compared by bees.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, particularly experiments 4 and 5.

claim: Once bees experience one option, in order to utilise the absolute information, they must experience a second option within several minutes.
source: That is, once bees experience one option, in order to utilise the absolute information, they must experience a second option within several minutes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, particularly experiments 4 and 5.

claim: With short inter-flower visits, bees can utilise absolute information in order to compare and rank flowers.
source: Both our proof-of-concept experiment (experiment 6) and other previous multi-choice semi-realistic foraging tasks (e.g. Greggers and Menzel, 1993) show that with short inter-flower visits, bees can utilise absolute information in order to compare and rank flowers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from experiment 6 and citations to previous research.

claim: If bees' choices were a result of state-dependent valuation learning (SDVL), then their preferences should be quantitative.
source: If bees' choices were a result of SDVL instead of remembered ordinal ranking, then their preferences should be quantitative, i.e. larger values should be assigned with larger differences between internal state and flower experience.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the SDVL mechanism.

claim: The results of experiment 3 speak against the interpretation that bees' choices are a result of state-dependent valuation learning.
source: However, the results of experiment 3 speak against this interpretation because bees were indifferent between equally ranked A and C even though they were experienced in a richer and poorer environment, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 3 in relation to the SDVL hypothesis.

claim: Breadth of diet has been suggested to play a role in the evolution of cognition.
source: Breadth of diet has been suggested to play a role in the evolution of cognition (Hemingway et al., 2017; MacLean et al., 2014; Simons and Tibbetts, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Humans and starlings forage on a range of different foods, whereas adult bumblebees feed almost exclusively on nectar and pollen from flowers.
source: Humans and starlings forage on a range of different foods, whereas adult bumblebees feed almost exclusively on nectar and pollen from flowers.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about the diets of these species.

claim: A varied diet, whereby one might need a common currency across vastly different food types, may have forced some animals to retain and use absolute memories.
source: Perhaps a varied diet, whereby one might need a common currency across vastly different food types (Chib et al., 2009; Levy and Glimcher, 2012) may have forced some animals to retain and use absolute memories, whereas a limited diet and limited dimensionality of reward might have favoured memories for ordinal relationships alone.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors, with supporting citations.

claim: A limited diet and limited dimensionality of reward might have favoured memories for ordinal relationships alone.
source: Perhaps a varied diet, whereby one might need a common currency across vastly different food types (Chib et al., 2009; Levy and Glimcher, 2012) may have forced some animals to retain and use absolute memories, whereas a limited diet and limited dimensionality of reward might have favoured memories for ordinal relationships alone.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: There is no reason yet to suggest a bee's brain lacks the neural substrates to retain and recall absolute memories for options for later use in novel contexts.
source: There is no reason yet to suggest a bee's brain lacks the neural substrates to retain and recall absolute memories for options for later use in novel contexts.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding bee neurobiology.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings on the gustatory neurons of bumblebees demonstrated that the spiking rates of these peripheral sensory neurons increased as a function of sucrose concentration.
source: In fact, recent electrophysiological recordings on the gustatory neurons of bumblebees demonstrated that the spiking rates of these peripheral sensory neurons increased as a function of sucrose concentration (Miriyala et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Gustatory neuronal signals could theoretically be used by higher centres of an animal's brain to encode an option's utility as a cardinal (absolute) value.
source: These gustatory neuronal signals could theoretically be used by higher centres of an animal's brain to encode an option's utility as a cardinal (absolute) value (Schultz, 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility based on cited research.

claim: Bumblebees do not access or utilise any potentially stored absolute memories when it would be of benefit in novel contexts.
source: However, our results suggest that bumblebees do not access or utilise any potentially stored absolute memories when it would be of benefit in novel contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental results presented.

claim: The findings demonstrate a fundamental difference in the mechanisms underlying learned preferences between those of bumblebees and those of starlings and humans.
source: Whatever the ultimate and proximate causes of bumblebees' ordinal-only memories for options' values, our findings demonstrate a fundamental difference in the mechanisms underlying learned preferences between those of bumblebees and those of starlings and humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the experimental results with previous research on starlings and humans.

claim: Bumblebee colonies were obtained from the Chinese branch of the Biobest Group.
source: Bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) colonies were obtained from the Chinese branch of the Biobest Group (Biobest Belgium N.V., Westerlo, Belgium) and housed in wooden nest boxes (28 cm × 16 cm × 11 cm).
evidence: This is a description of the materials and methods used in the study.

claim: Experimental design and procedures were guided by the 3Rs principles (replacement, reduction, and refinement).
source: Although there are no current requirements regarding insect care and use in research, experimental design and procedures were guided by the 3Rs principles (replacement, reduction, and refinement; Russell and Burch, 1959).
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical considerations of the study, with a citation to the 3Rs principles.

claim: The behavioural tests were non-invasive.
source: The behavioural tests were non-invasive, and the types of manipulations used (sucrose and water) are all experienced by bumblebees during their natural foraging life in the wild.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The types of manipulations used (sucrose and water) are all experienced by bumblebees during their natural foraging life in the wild.
source: The behavioural tests were non-invasive, and the types of manipulations used (sucrose and water) are all experienced by bumblebees during their natural foraging life in the wild.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about bumblebee foraging behavior.

claim: Colonies were fed outside of experiments with 5–15% sucrose solution (w/w).
source: To ensure the sucrose solution concentration used in experiments was motivating, colonies were fed outside of experiments with 5–15% sucrose solution (w/w).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Colonies were provided with ~3 g pollen every day.
source: They were also provided with ~3 g pollen every day.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The minimal perceptual distance of all the colour combinations used in this study was above 0.14 hexagon units, which can be well differentiated by bumblebees.
source: The minimal perceptual distance of all the colour combinations used in this study was above 0.14 hexagon units, which can be well differentiated by bumblebees (Dyer and Chittka, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research on bumblebee color discrimination.

claim: Neurophysiological and behavioural evidence verify that the sugar concentration differences used in this study can be readily discriminated by bumblebees.
source: Furthermore, neurophysiological (Miriyala et al., 2018) and behavioural evidence (Whitney et al., 2008) verify that the sugar concentration differences used in this study can be readily discriminated by bumblebees.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Training was completed when a bee collected 50 of the 20 μl aliquots of sugar reward from flowers of both colours.
source: Training was completed when a bee collected 50 of the 20 μl aliquots of sugar reward from flowers of both colours.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: In all tests, the two flowers types presented had not been experienced previously together in the same arena by the bees.
source: Note that in all tests, the two flowers types presented had not been experienced previously together in the same arena by the bees.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: R v.3.6.1 was used to perform all GLMs with quasibinomial distribution and logit link function.
source: R v.3.6.1 was used to perform all GLMs with quasibinomial distribution and logit link function.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: For all models, the response variable was the proportion of choices for the flower that had been associated with high concentration sugar water.
source: For all models, the response variable was the proportion of choices for the flower that had been associated with high concentration sugar water.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: Fixed factors for models for results of experiments were (i) colony of each bee, (ii) flower colour, and (iii) training sequence.
source: Fixed factors for models for results of experiments were (i) colony of each bee, (ii) flower colour, and (iii) training sequence (whether the higher concentration sugar reward was used during the first or second training session).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: None of the fixed effects were found to have a significant effect on bees' preferences during the tests in any experiment.
source: Significance of fixed effects was tested using likelihood ratio tests, and none were found to have a significant effect on bees' preferences during the tests in any experiment.
evidence: This is a result of the statistical analysis.

claim: Bumblebees were able to learn to discriminate between two differently coloured flowers in the experimental setup.
source: To ensure that bees were able to learn to discriminate between two differently coloured flowers in our setup, we examined bees' preference between two flower types after having been trained individually on these flowers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Bees showed a clear preference for flowers that had been associated with the higher reward during training (generalised linear model [GLM]: N=20, 95% CI = [0.64, 1.37], and p=3.39e-5).
source: During a subsequent unrewarded test (all flowers with unrewarding water), bees showed a clear preference for (landed more often on) the flowers that had been associated with the higher reward during training (generalised linear model [GLM]: N=20, 95% CI = [0.64, 1.37], and p=3.39e-5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Bumblebees were able to easily learn to discriminate the different flower colours used in the experiments via the different sucrose concentrations associated with each flower type.
source: These results show that in our setup, bumblebees were able to easily learn to discriminate the different flower colours used in our experiments and do so via the different sucrose concentrations associated with each flower type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: If bumblebees encode and retrieve memories for absolute values, their preference for a particular option should not depend on the context in which that option was learned.
source: If bumblebees encode and retrieve memories for absolute values, their preference for a particular option should not depend on the context in which that option was learned (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on cited research about absolute value encoding.

claim: If bumblebees' preferences were driven exclusively by their memory for absolute values for options, they should show no preference between B and C in the test of experiment 1.
source: Therefore, if bumblebees' preferences were driven exclusively by their memory for absolute values for options, they should show no preference between B and C in the test.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the experimental design of experiment 1.

claim: Any significant preference between B and C in experiment 1 would suggest a contextual effect due to B and C having different rankings during training.
source: Any significant preference would suggest a contextual effect due to B and C having different rankings during training (B<A while C>D).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the experimental design of experiment 1.

claim: If bumblebees retain and use memories for both ranking and absolute information (and the value weights for these two different types of information are not extremely unbalanced), bees should either prefer B over C because it is much higher in quality, or this value difference would cancel out the ranking difference.
source: If bumblebees retain and use memories for both ranking and absolute information (and the value weights for these two different types of information are not extremely unbalanced), bees should either prefer B over C because it is much higher in quality, or this value difference would cancel out the ranking difference (B<A while C>D), and their preference for B and C should be equal.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the experimental design of experiment 2.

claim: A preference for the much lower reward quality flower C in experiment 2 would indicate bees have access to only ranking memories.
source: On the other hand, a preference for the much lower reward quality flower C would indicate they have access to only ranking memories.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the experimental design of experiment 2.

claim: A preference for C over B in experiments 1 and 2 may have resulted from remembered ranking or a distorted absolute memory for flower type B due to the presence of and comparison with A during training.
source: Note that a preference for C over B in experiments 1 and 2 may have resulted from remembered ranking or a distorted absolute memory for flower type B due to the presence of and comparison with A during training.
evidence: This is a consideration of alternative explanations for the experimental results.

claim: If bees encode memories for relative differences in quantitative terms, C should be preferred over A in experiment 3.
source: If bees encode memories for relative differences in quantitative terms, C should be preferred over A, as C had a higher relative value than A.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the experimental design of experiment 3.

claim: If bees only remember the ordinal rank of options, preference for A and C should be the same in experiment 3 because they have the same rank within their training contexts.
source: Alternatively, if bees only remember the ordinal rank of options, preference for A and C should be the same because they have the same rank within their training contexts.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the experimental design of experiment 3.

claim: Because the two flower types in experiment 4 were separated physically and temporally, bees had no ranking information available to putatively overshadow absolute information.
source: Because the two flower types were separated physically and temporally, bees had no ranking information available to putatively overshadow absolute information.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design of experiment 4.

claim: Any preferences formed in experiment 4 would be a result of remembered absolute information.
source: Therefore, any preferences formed would be a result of remembered absolute information.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the experimental design of experiment 4.

claim: During training in experiments 1–3, bumblebees could see flowers of both types simultaneously.
source: During training in experiments 1–3, bumblebees could see flowers of both types simultaneously.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design of experiments 1-3.

claim: In experiment 5, both flower types were never in a bee's visual field at the same time.
source: This way, both flower types were never in a bee's visual field at the same time.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design of experiment 5.

claim: In experiment 6, bumblebees learned to forage from flowers of four different colours but could only see flowers of two colours at any one time.
source: Here, in a divided arena, bumblebees learned to forage from flowers of four different colours (Figure 2E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3) but could only see flowers of two colours at any one time, i.e. could only see A and B (45% and 30%) flowers from one side of the arena and could only see C and D (30% and 20%) flowers from the other side (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design of experiment 6.
